name: Design a Progressive Delivery Platform
intent: Move a new version of a service from zero to all users in careful stages, one region at a time, judge each stage by comparing live metrics with the old version, and undo it automatically, so a bad release harms a few users for a few minutes.
codeTitle: a staged canary rollout with a z-test gate
finalIntro: One release of a checkout service crossing its first region, and the next one being stopped.
prompt: Design the platform behind our releases. 400 services deploy about 400 times a day, to 6 regions. A release must grow from 1% of traffic to everyone, in stages and in region waves, and the platform itself must decide, from live metrics, whether to continue or to roll back. Teams also use feature flags, and some releases need a human to approve them.
functional: Shift traffic to a new version in stages, such as 1%, 10%, 50% and 100%
Compare the new version with the old one on error rate, latency and business metrics
Roll back automatically when the comparison fails, and let a person pause, resume or roll back by hand
Roll out region by region, with a wait (bake time) between stages and waves
Work together with feature flags, and keep database changes safe to undo
Require approvals, freezes and an audit trail for risky releases
nonFunctional: A bad release is detected and removed within minutes, while it is still on a few percent of one region
Few false rollbacks, so teams trust the platform and do not bypass it
A hard limit on how many users one release can ever reach before a decision
The controller keeps working, or stops safely, when metrics or the controller itself fail
Hundreds of rollouts at once with a small, predictable load on the metrics system
Every decision can be explained afterwards with the numbers behind it

firstAttempt.text: A deploy script replaces the old version on every host in every region, then runs a health check, and an engineer watches a dashboard. If the dashboard looks bad, they run the script again with the previous version.
limits: Every user gets the bad version at once, so the damage is as large as it can be
A health check only proves the process started, not that checkout still works for real users
A human watching a graph is slow and inconsistent, and nobody watches 400 releases a day
Going back means another full deploy, so the outage lasts as long as the rollout did
Nothing limits blast radius, nothing records what was decided and why, and a database change may not be reversible

steps.title: Shift traffic in stages instead of replacing everything
steps.problem: Replacing the old version everywhere at once exposes every user to a bug before anyone can see it, and going back takes as long as going forward.
steps.fix: Run the new version next to the old one, as a small canary group of instances, and let a traffic router send it a chosen share of requests: 1%, then 10%, then 50%, then everything. The router is a weighted load balancer, service mesh or gateway, and the share is a number in its configuration, so changing it takes seconds and going back means setting the weight to zero while the old version is still running. Choose users by a hash of a stable id, so a user stays on one version during the rollout instead of flipping between them on every request.
steps.tradeoff: At any moment the damage is limited to the current share, and the old version is the instant fallback. The cost is extra capacity while both versions run, two versions that must work with the same data, and slower releases than a single push.

steps.title: Compare the canary with the stable version using statistics
steps.problem: A canary only helps if something decides whether it is healthy, and a fixed limit such as 'errors below 2%' goes wrong when the whole system has a bad minute.
steps.fix: Collect the same metrics for both groups, tagged with the version: error rate, latency percentiles, saturation and a business metric such as completed checkouts. Compare them at the same time and for the same kind of traffic, so a shared problem hits both and cancels out. For a rate use a one-sided two-proportion test, with the pooled error rate and a z limit of about 2.3, and for latency compare a percentile with a test that does not assume a normal shape. Do not decide before the canary has seen enough requests, around 300 at the least. The number needed grows when the regression to detect is small: to see an error rate go from 1% to 2% takes close to 3,000 requests in each group. For a clean baseline, start a fresh group of old-version instances as large as the canary, instead of comparing with the whole old fleet that has been warm for days.
steps.tradeoff: The decision is based on evidence and survives noise that hits everyone. It takes time to collect enough requests, so a small stage on a quiet service may need a long wait, and each extra metric tested raises the chance of a false alarm unless the limits are set for it.

steps.title: Let a controller advance, wait and roll back by itself
steps.problem: If a person must read the numbers and press the button, the rollback comes after a coffee break, and 400 releases a day cannot be watched.
steps.fix: A rollout controller runs the plan as a state machine: set the weight, wait the bake time, ask the analysis for a verdict, and then advance, hold or roll back. Pass moves to the next stage. Fail sets the weight to zero, scales the canary down and marks the release failed with the numbers that caused it. Inconclusive extends the wait until there is enough data, up to a limit. The bake time between stages matters as much as the stage sizes, since problems such as slow leaks or cold caches take time to show. The state of every rollout is saved, so a restarted controller resumes where it was, and people can pause, resume or roll back by hand.
steps.tradeoff: Rollback takes seconds and needs no human, and every release is judged by the same rules. A wrong rule now stops many releases, so the thresholds need an owner, a way to override and a record of the false alarms. A longer bake time is safer but slows every release.

steps.title: Roll out region by region, and cap the blast radius
steps.problem: A bug that passes a canary in one region can still fail somewhere else, and a rollout that touches six regions in parallel loses all the protection of going slowly.
steps.fix: Divide the release into waves: first a small, low-risk region or cell, then a few more, then the big ones. A wave starts only when the one before it finished its stages and has baked. The controller enforces limits that no team can skip: the highest share of global traffic that may be on a new version at once, the number of regions in flight, and no rollout while the service is spending its error budget too fast or an incident is open. Each region, and ideally each cell inside it, keeps its own router and metrics, so a failure stays inside one.
steps.tradeoff: The worst case becomes a known fraction of users, such as 1% of one region. A release now takes hours rather than minutes, and urgent fixes need a fast lane with its own approval, since the slow path is the safe one.

steps.title: Combine deploys with feature flags and keep data changes reversible
steps.problem: A rollback of the code does not undo everything: a database column may have changed, a new feature may already have written data, and some bugs live in one feature rather than in the whole release.
steps.fix: Separate shipping code from exposing behaviour. The code goes out through the canary with the new feature behind a flag that is off, so the metrics test the code path with no change in behaviour. Afterwards the flag is turned on in its own stages, and a flag change is a rollout too, with its own comparison and its own instant undo. Do not change a flag during a canary analysis, so cause and effect stay clear. For data, use the expand and contract pattern: add the new column first, write both, read the new one, and drop the old one in a later release, so the old version always still works with the data.
steps.tradeoff: A bad feature can be removed in seconds without redeploying, and rollbacks stay safe. Flags and migrations add a second thing to track, flags must be cleaned up, and the extra steps make data changes span several releases.

steps.title: Add approvals, freezes and an audit trail
steps.problem: Some releases carry more risk than others, a company has times when nothing should change, and after an incident people need to know who released what and why the platform decided as it did.
steps.fix: A release policy, kept as code and itself reviewed, says what each service needs: a plain release may start by itself, a risky one needs an approver from another team, a payment service needs a change ticket. Freeze windows such as a sale day block starts but never stop a rollback. The controller records every step in an append-only audit log: who started it, who approved, the version, each stage with the numbers and the verdict, and any manual override. Only the platform can change weights in production, and the build must come from a trusted pipeline with a signed artifact.
steps.tradeoff: Risky changes get a second pair of eyes and every decision can be explained. Approvals slow people down and can turn into a rubber stamp, so they are used for risk and not for everything, and the break-glass path is allowed but loud.

failures.scenario: The canary gets only a few requests, so the numbers are noise
failures.impact: With 20 requests a single error looks like a 5% error rate: the platform either rolls back a good release or approves a bad one.
failures.answer: The analysis refuses to decide below a minimum number of requests and says 'inconclusive'. The controller then extends the bake time, raises the share for the next stage, or, for a service that gets very little traffic, sends synthetic requests to the canary. The limit is stated per service in the policy.

failures.scenario: The metrics system is late or down during a rollout
failures.impact: The analysis has no data, and a controller that treats 'no errors seen' as 'healthy' would promote a broken release.
failures.answer: Missing or stale data is never a pass. The controller holds the current stage, raises an alert, and after a limit rolls back to the last known good state. The metrics are also read from the canary's own health signals as a second source, and a rollout never advances while the data is older than a few minutes.

failures.scenario: A memory leak shows up only after an hour at full traffic
failures.impact: The release passed every stage, since the leak needs time and load to matter, and now the whole fleet is slowly running out of memory.
failures.answer: Saturation metrics such as memory growth per hour are part of the comparison, the last stage before 100% has a longer soak, and the first hours after promotion are watched with the same analysis and an instant rollback. A leak still in the canary is visible as a trend, and not as a level, so the analysis checks slope too.

failures.scenario: The new version wrote data that the old version cannot read
failures.impact: The rollback succeeds on paper, and then the old version crashes on the records the canary created.
failures.answer: Releases follow expand and contract: new fields are optional, the old version ignores what it does not know, and a field is only removed one release after nothing reads it. The platform blocks promotion of a release that contains a contract step until the previous release has been stable for a set time, and the check 'can the previous version read this data' is part of the review.

failures.scenario: The rollout controller crashes in the middle of a wave
failures.impact: The weight is stuck at 10% in two regions, nobody is watching, and a bad release could sit there.
failures.answer: Rollout state is stored durably after every transition, and several controller replicas elect a leader with a lease. The new leader reads the state and continues, and because each step is idempotent (set the weight to 10, not raise it by 10), repeating a step is harmless. A rollout that makes no progress past its deadline pages the owner and falls back to the stable version.

alternatives.title: How traffic is shifted

options.name: Weighted routing in a mesh or gateway
options.pro: Exact percentages, per-request or per-user stickiness, and a change takes seconds
options.con: Needs a routing layer in the path of every service

options.name: Rolling update of instances
options.pro: Built into the orchestrator and needs no extra capacity
options.con: The share is the share of instances, it is coarse, and the old version is gone as it goes

options.name: Weighted DNS records
options.pro: Works anywhere and without a proxy
options.con: Slow to change because of caches, with uneven shares and no sticky users

alternatives.pick: Weighted routing for services in a mesh or behind a gateway, and rolling updates for simple internal tools.

alternatives.title: How the verdict is decided

options.name: Fixed thresholds
options.pro: Simple to explain and to write
options.con: Wrong when the whole system is noisy, and they need tuning per service

options.name: Statistical test against a live baseline
options.pro: Cancels shared noise, and has a stated false-alarm rate
options.con: Needs enough requests, and many metrics make more false alarms

options.name: Learned anomaly model
options.pro: Can pick up complicated patterns across many metrics
options.con: Hard to explain to the owner of a blocked release, and needs history

alternatives.pick: A statistical comparison for the few metrics that matter, plus hard limits as a safety net.

alternatives.title: What the canary is compared with

options.name: The whole stable fleet
options.pro: A large sample and nothing extra to run
options.con: Old instances are warm, different in size and age, so differences can come from that

options.name: A fresh baseline group started with the canary
options.pro: Same age, same size, same cache state, so the only difference is the code
options.con: Costs extra instances for the length of the rollout

options.name: Historical data from last week
options.con: Traffic mix and events change, so it blames the release for the weekday

alternatives.pick: A fresh baseline of the same size for important services, the whole fleet for the rest.

alternatives.title: Canary or blue-green

options.name: Canary in stages
options.pro: Limits exposure and tests with real traffic gradually
options.con: Two versions run for a long time, and it needs enough traffic to measure

options.name: Blue-green switch
options.pro: A clean cut with an instant switch back, and the new fleet can be tested before it gets users
options.con: All users move at once, so a bug that tests miss reaches everyone, and it needs double capacity

alternatives.pick: Canary stages by default. Blue-green for changes that cannot run side by side, such as a breaking protocol change.
